title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to evaluate whether an automated generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The run used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) under adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation semantics and a primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution completed all planned pairs (complete_pair_count = 200), consuming 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued because every initial candidate passed the validator. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; estimate = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). A preregistered 10% Mininet holdout produced zero validator–emulator disagreements. Because baseline validator failures were absent on this task bank under the frozen generation policy, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. We report the sealed design, deterministic execution accounting, and an artifact‑grounded interpretation and limitations emphasizing workload dependence of GVR utility (preregistration id: cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02).

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation with large language models offers productivity gains for network operations but risks producing incorrect or unsafe changes that cause outages or policy violations. To mitigate these risks, prior proposals combine LLM generation with deterministic validators and repair loops (generate–validate–repair, GVR). The practical safety benefit of automated repair depends on (1) the baseline prevalence of validator‑detectable failures under the chosen generator and prompting policy, (2) validator coverage and fidelity, and (3) the available repair budget and repair‑prompt effectiveness. We preregistered a narrowly scoped confirmatory question and a paired design: does a deterministic GVR pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator materially reduce validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only pipeline on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank when the same initial generator output is shared across conditions?
sections.related_work: Empirical studies and surveys document LLM factual errors, hallucinations, prompt sensitivity, and non‑determinism; mitigation techniques include retrieval grounding, verifier‑assisted repair, constrained agent designs, and guarded tool use. NetOps prototypes and intent→configuration systems demonstrate feasibility but rarely report instrumented, preregistered failure‑rate evaluations under controlled causal contrasts. Red‑team audits and configuration‑brittleness studies show that agentic workflows and tool descriptions can materially change safety outcomes. Our confirmatory experiment contributes an externally auditable, preregistered measurement that isolates the marginal effect of deterministic validator‑assisted repair on identical generator outputs, addressing a gap about when deterministic GVR reduces validator‑detectable failures in practice.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and inferential plan. The preregistered plan (cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02) specified a paired design with n = 200 tasks, one shared deterministic initial generation per task, and a repair budget of at most one automated repair call per task. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline and the primary test was the exact two‑sided McNemar test (α = 0.05). Bootstrap percentile 95% CIs used 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). Power planning assumed baseline unsafe incidence ≈30% and a target 50% relative reduction; sample size selection is recorded in the preregistration.

Task bank and validators. We used a curated, machine‑checkable intent→configuration bank (200 tasks across four topology clusters: enterprise, campus, datacenter, edge; 50 tasks each). Each task encodes initial/final states, workflow constraints (make‑before‑break, must_be_down_for_fields, group minima), and a required_sequence checked by the primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), which enforces syntactic and intent/constraint checks and emits structured diagnostics (valid flag, violation codes, parsed_command_count, required_command_count).

Shared‑initial adapter semantics and determinism reconciliation. The hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter enforced shared_initial generation semantics: a single initial candidate was produced and reused for both baseline and guarded conditions for each task to isolate the marginal effect of invoking validation and (if needed) repair on the same output. Execution artifacts confirm that arrangement: completed_episode_count = 400 (shared reuse across the two conditions), model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task), and provider audit fields indicate hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}. The provider metadata file records "temperature": null; determinism for the paired contrast was therefore achieved by adapter enforcement of a single shared call per task rather than by relying on a provider temperature metadata field. The deterministic_reconciliation and execution accounting artifacts document these enforced adapter semantics and per‑task single invocations.

Repair, contamination, and emulation checks. The preregistered repair policy allowed one automated repair call when the primary validator reported violations; repair candidates would be re‑validated by deterministic_netops_validator_v5. A Mininet‑based data‑plane emulator was preregistered as a secondary disagreement detector and applied to a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) to detect validator–emulator mismatches. Any disagreement would be flagged and, per the preregistered contamination plan, excluded from the primary analysis; artifacts record the contamination summary for that holdout. All seeds, logs, and artifacts referenced below are archived in the execution bundle for audit (see archival pointer).
sections.results:
Execution and accounting. The autonomous run executed under the frozen plan (start: 2026‑08‑30T11:50:34.530059Z; end: 2026‑08‑30T12:12:07.541650Z). Completed_episode_count = 400, complete_pair_count = 200, model_calls_used = 200, maximum_model_calls permitted = 400, repair_calls_used = 0. Provider accounting confirms hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}, verifying single shared initial invocation per task.

Primary outcomes and exact inference. Every initial candidate passed the primary deterministic validator: baseline_success_count = 200/200 and guarded_success_count = 200/200. The paired contingency table is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The observed paired difference estimate = 0.0. The prespecified exact two‑sided McNemar test yields p = 1.0. Bootstrap percentile confidence intervals (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) produce a 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. Because the baseline validator failure rate was 0% on this task bank under the frozen generation policy, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated here.

Mininet holdout and contamination. The preregistered 10% Mininet holdout (20 tasks) produced zero validator–emulator disagreements according to the contamination summary artifact. We disclose a reproducibility gap: the labeled artifact set does not include an explicit selection seed identifying the exact task indices drawn for the Mininet holdout, which prevents bit‑for‑bit reconstruction of that holdout draw despite the contamination summary reporting zero disagreements.

Secondary estimands and repairs. No validator failures occurred; consequently the repair branch was never invoked and preregistered secondary estimands (average repair iterations, GVR‑introduced failure rate, model‑call cost per successful repair) have no empirical observations in this run and are recorded as empty in the archived analysis artifacts.
sections.discussion:
Conditional interpretation. The degenerate null (zero baseline validator failures) is an artifact‑grounded outcome: under the frozen shared‑initial generation policy and the chosen LLM and prompts, every generated candidate satisfied the deterministic validator for the curated task bank. This result is not proof that GVR is universally unnecessary; it precisely states that, for this combination of workload, generator/prompt policy, and validator, there were no validator‑detectable failures for the GVR pipeline to reduce.

Methodological trade‑offs and practical implications. The shared_initial paired design isolates the incremental effect of invoking validator+repair on a fixed generator output but intentionally excludes any benefit obtainable by re‑sampling the LLM (e.g., producing alternative candidates that a repair could act upon). For operational risk estimation (unconditional failure prevalence), designs with independent per‑condition sampling and multiple draws per task are more informative. Practitioners should therefore: (1) measure baseline validator failure prevalence for representative production workloads under the intended generation policy; (2) expand validator fidelity (vendor/device models, emulation coverage); and (3) consider multi‑sample and multi‑step repair budgets when baseline failures are nontrivial.

Validator fidelity and emulator corroboration. Deterministic validators codify a specific set of syntactic and policy checks; they can miss device idiosyncrasies or end‑to‑end failures only observable at the data plane. The Mininet holdout was included to probe such blind spots; the zero disagreements observed in the small holdout increase confidence for this run but do not substitute for larger emulation or real‑device testing. The missing labeled selection seed for the holdout reduces exact reproducibility of that corroboration and is explicitly disclosed as a reproducibility gap.

Statistical mechanics in the degenerate paired case. When discordant counts are zero the McNemar test is degenerate and conveys that no paired improvement was observed on the sampled pairs; bootstrap percentile intervals centered at zero (here [0.0, 0.0]) reflect that absence of variation under the resampling procedure used. This outcome underscores that confirmatory power depends on baseline failure prevalence and on design choices that permit sampling variability when that variability is relevant to the estimand of interest.

Recommendations for future confirmatory studies. To characterize GVR effectiveness where baseline failures are rare, future preregistered runs should (i) include independent per‑condition multi‑sample draws to estimate unconditional failure rates; (ii) increase repair budgets and permit multi‑step repairs or human escalation; (iii) scale secondary emulation checks and record selection seeds for exact reproducibility; and (iv) evaluate multiple models or ensembles to probe model‑dependent brittleness. The archived execution and analysis artifacts provide concrete accounting patterns and audit templates for such extensions.
sections.conclusion: We executed a sealed, preregistered paired study comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 NetOps intent→configuration tasks using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs), yielding an observed paired difference of 0.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0, and bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. The preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be evaluated because baseline validator failures were absent. This artifact‑grounded outcome clarifies that GVR’s marginal value is workload dependent: when baseline validator‑detectable failures are rare under the production generator/prompt policy, a single‑pass automated repair yields no measured benefit for those validator‑detected errors. Future work should focus on workloads with nontrivial baseline failure rates, richer validator/emulator coverage, multi‑sample generation policies, and expanded repair budgets to characterize operational gains.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure (mandatory). This study executed under the autonomous post‑lock preregistration cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02. Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini (provider label: openai_responses) invoked via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter. The exact initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Topic constraints: the human Research Director limited the study to Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps focusing on safety/reliability of generated network changes. Orchestration and task generation used hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Primary deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Preregistration and freeze: the experimental plan (estimand, sample size n = 200, paired design, stopping rules, max model calls = 400, repair budget = 1 per task, shared‑initial semantics) was frozen before any model calls. Autonomous execution: the run executed under the frozen plan (start: 2026‑08‑30T11:50:34.530059Z; end: 2026‑08‑30T12:12:07.541650Z). Execution accounting: completed_episode_count = 400, complete_pair_count = 200, model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task), repair_calls_used = 0. Determinism reconciliation: adapter enforcement produced single shared invocations per task as evidenced by provider audit fields showing hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}; the provider metadata includes "temperature": null but determinism for the paired contrast was achieved by adapter semantics rather than by relying on a provider temperature value. Contamination/emulation: a preregistered Mininet holdout (10%, 20 tasks) was executed as an independent disagreement detector and produced zero validator–emulator disagreements in the archived contamination summary; a reproducibility gap exists because the explicit labeled selection seed for that holdout is not present in the labeled artifacts. Human involvement: the human Research Director selected the topic family and pre‑lock constraints; no human manual editing or selective rewriting of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock. Deviations and restarts: no post‑preregistration design changes or technical restarts occurred.
limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested (completed accounting shows model_calls_used = 200 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}). Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
